Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 68, verses 8–16:

Allah's words: ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾. The reason was that the leaders of the people of Makkah invited him to the religion of his forefathers, so Allah forbade him to obey them. ﴿They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾. There are seven opinions concerning this.

The first: "That you would grant concessions, so they would grant concessions," said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "That you would flatter them regarding your religion, so they would flatter them regarding their religion," said by al-Hasan.

The third: "That you would disbelieve, so they would disbelieve," said by 'Atiyyah, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil.

The fourth: "That you would be lenient, so they would be lenient toward you," said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The fifth: "That you would be hypocritical and show off, so they would be hypocritical and show off," said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The sixth: "They wish that you would be pliant in your religion, so they would be pliant in their religions." They had wanted him to worship their gods for a period, and they would worship Allah for a period, said by Ibn Qutaybah. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is from al-mudahana (flattery/pliancy).

The seventh: "That you would draw near to them, so they would draw near to you," said by Ibn Kaysan.

Allah's words: ﴿And do not obey every oath-maker﴾, one who swears much by falsehood. ﴿Contemptible﴾, meaning the base, the lowly. al-'Awfi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: al-mahin is the liar.

They differed regarding who this verse was revealed about, in three opinions.

The first: that it is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. The second: al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, said by 'Ata' and al-Suddi. The third: al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, said by Mujahid.

Allah's words: ﴿Backbiter﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he is the one who slanders. Ibn Qutaybah said: he is the one who finds fault.

Allah's words: ﴿Going about with slander﴾, meaning he walks among the people carrying tale-bearing, which is conveying evil speech from some of them to others in order to sow discord among them. ﴿Hindering the good﴾, concerning which there are two opinions.

The first: that he prevented his son and his clan from Islam, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: he withheld the rights in his wealth, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Allah's words: ﴿Transgressor﴾, meaning oppressive. ﴿Sinful﴾, wicked. ﴿Brutal after that﴾, meaning in addition to what We have described him with. Concerning "brutal" there are seven opinions.

The first: that he is the harsh, severe hypocrite, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that he is the one of stout body, said by al-Hasan. The third: the severe and arrogant, said by Mujahid. The fourth: the strong in his disbelief, said by 'Ikrimah. The fifth: the great eater, the great drinker, the strong and severe, said by 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr. The sixth: the severe in quarrelling falsely, said by al-Farra'. The seventh: that he is the coarse, harsh one, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Concerning "zanim" (illegitimate, one attached) there are four opinions.

The first: that he is the one claimed as a kinsman among Quraysh though he is not one of them, narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas. This is well known in the language: the zanim is the one who attaches himself to a people though he is not of them. This was said by al-Farra', Abu 'Ubaydah, and Ibn Qutaybah. Hassan said:

"You are a zanim, attached to the family of Hashim, as the single cup is hung behind the rider."

The second: that he is the one known for evil, as a sheep is known by its zanama (dangling ear-tag), narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that he has a zanama like the zanama of a sheep. Ibn 'Abbas said: he was described but was not recognized until it was said "zanim," and then he was recognized, for he had a zanama on his neck by which he was known. We know of no one whose faults Allah mentioned more thoroughly than those of al-Walid, for He described him with swearing, base conduct, finding fault with people, walking about with tale-bearing, miserliness, oppression, sin, harshness, and illegitimate claim, so He attached to him a shame that does not leave him in this world or the Hereafter. The two zanamat are the two hangings at the throats of goats. Ibn Faris said: it means the one that hangs from its ear.

The fourth: that he is the oppressor, narrated by al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas.

Allah's words: ﴿Because he possesses wealth and sons﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read "an kana" as a statement (i.e., "because he was"). The meaning: do not obey him for his wealth and sons. Ibn 'Abbas read it with two hamzas, the first light and the second softened, and Abu Ja'far separated them with an alif. Hamzah read "a-an kana" with two light hamzas as an interrogative, and it has two readings.

The first: "Because he possessed wealth, would you obey him?!"

The second: "Because he possessed wealth and sons?! When Our verses are recited to him, does he disbelieve in them, and say: 'Fables of the ancients'?" al-Farra' mentioned both interpretations. Ibn Mas'ud read "an kana" with one shortened hamza.

Then He threatened him, saying: ﴿We will brand him upon the snout﴾. Al-Khurtum means the nose. There are three opinions concerning this branding.

The first: "We will brand him with the sword, making that a mark on his nose for as long as he lives." He fought on the day of Badr, and his nose was struck with a sword, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "We will attach to him something that will not leave him," said by Qatadah, and preferred by Ibn Qutaybah.

The third: the meaning is that We will blacken his face. Al-Farra' said: although al-khurtum has been specifically applied to a brand, it carries the sense of "face," since part of the face stands for the whole. Al-Zajjaj said: We will make for him in the Hereafter the mark by which the people of the Fire are recognized, through the blackening of their faces. It is permissible, and Allah knows best, that he be singled out with a mark because of his extreme enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), by which he is distinguished from others.

[p-336] The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have tested them﴾ means the people of Makkah, that is, We tested them with hunger and famine, ﴿as We tested the owners of the garden﴾ when their garden was destroyed.

This is a reference to their story. The people of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) mentioned that there was a man in the region of Yemen who had a garden, and he was a believer. This was after 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon them both. He would take from it only enough for his sustenance and would give away the rest in charity. It was also said that he would leave for the poor what the sickle passed over, what fell from the tops of the palm trees, and what scattered during threshing. A considerable amount would accumulate from this. Then the man died and left three sons. They said: "By God, the wealth is little and the dependents are many. Our father only did this when the wealth was abundant and the dependents few, but now we cannot do this." So they resolved to deprive the poor, and they made a pact among themselves that they would go out early, before people went out, and cut their palm trees. This is the meaning of His statement: ﴿when they swore﴾, that is, they took an oath, ﴿that they would surely harvest it﴾, that is, they would surely cut their palm trees, ﴿in the early morning﴾, that is, at the first light of dawn. Some darkness of the night still remained, so that nothing would be left for the poor.

Regarding His statement ﴿and they did not make an exception﴾ there are two views.

The first: they did not say, "If God wills." This is the view of most scholars.

The second: they did not make an exception for the right of the poor. This was said by 'Ikrimah.

[p-337] ﴿Then there passed over it a visitation from your Lord﴾, that is, from the command of your Lord. Al-Farra' said: the visitation can only occur at night. The exegetes said: God sent a fire upon it at night, and it was burned and became black. This is the meaning of His statement: ﴿so it became like the darkened [garden]﴾. On this there are three views.

The first: it became like black ash. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it became like the blackened night. This was said by al-Farra'. Likewise Ibn Qutaybah said: it became black like the night, burned. Al-Layl (the night) is also called al-sarim, and al-subh (the morning) is also called sarim, because each of them is cut off (yanṣarim) from the other.

The third: it became morning and the fruit in it had gone, so it was as if it had been cut off (ṣurima), that is, cut and harvested. This was also related by Ibn Qutaybah.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Then they called to one another at dawn﴾, that is, some of them called to others when they had risen in the morning, ["Go early to your tilth"], meaning the fruits, crops and grapes, ﴿if you are going to harvest﴾, that is, if you are going to cut the palm trees. ﴿So they set out﴾, that is, they went to their garden, ﴿while they whispered﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: they spoke secretly, [saying], ["No poor person shall enter it upon you today"], ﴿and they went early with determination﴾. On this there are eight views.

[p-338] The first: with capability. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: with want. This was said by al-Hasan in one narration.

The third: with seriousness. This was said by al-Hasan in another narration, and by Qatadah, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Farra', and Muqatil.

The fourth: with a matter that was agreed upon and that they had established among themselves. This was said by Mujahid and 'Ikrimah.

The fifth: that al-harad is the name of the garden. This was said by al-Suddi.

The sixth: that it is anger and wrath against the poor. This was said by al-Sha'bi and Sufyan. Abu 'Ubaydah recited:

"Lions of a den met the hidden lions,
they gave one another to drink, in anger, the blood of lions."

The seventh: that it is prevention, derived from "the year was harad" when there was no rain in it, and "the she-camel was harad" when she had no milk. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah.

The eighth: that it is intention. One says, "I haradtu your harad," meaning, I intended your intention. This was related by al-Farra', Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah. They recited:

"A torrent has come from the command of God,
it intends the intention of the garden that is closed off."

That is, it intends its intention. Ibn Qutaybah said: there are two dialects in it, harad and hard, as one says al-darak and al-darak.

Regarding His statement ﴿capable﴾ there are three views.

The first: capable of their garden in their own estimation. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: capable over the poor. This was said by al-Sha'bi.

The third: the meaning is that they prevented while they were able, that is, they had the means. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

They said, ﴿when they saw it﴾ burned, ﴿"Indeed, we have gone astray."﴾ That is, we have lost the way to our garden, for this is not it. Then they realized it was a punishment, so they said: ﴿"Rather, we are deprived."﴾ That is, we were deprived of the fruit of our garden by withholding from the poor. ﴿The most just of them said﴾, that is, the most upright and the best of them. ﴿"Why did you not"﴾, that is, "Would that you had," ﴿"glorify [God]"﴾. On this there are three views.

The first: "Why did you not make an exception when you said: ['We will surely harvest it in the early morning']." This was said by Ibn Jurayj and the majority. The meaning is: "Why did you not say, 'If God wills'?" Al-Zajjaj said: the exception was called glorification (tasbih), because tasbih in the language means exalting God, the Mighty and Majestic, above evil. The exception is a magnification of God and an acknowledgement that no one can do an act except by the will of God.

The second: their exception was the statement "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to God). This was said by Abu Salih.

The third: "Why do you not glorify God and thank Him for what He has given you?" This was related by al-Tha'labi.

[p-339] The statement of the Exalted: ﴿They said, "Glory be to our Lord"﴾, so they declared Him free from being unjust in what He did, and they confessed against themselves to wrongdoing, so they said: ﴿"Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾ By withholding from the poor. ["Then they turned to one another, blaming each other"], that is, some of them blamed others for withholding the rights of the poor. One says to another, "You advised us," and the other says, "You did it." Then they called out against themselves with woe, and they said: ﴿"Woe to us! Indeed, we were transgressors."﴾ Because we did not do what our fathers did. Then they returned to God the Exalted and asked Him to replace it for them with something better. This is the meaning of His statement: ﴿"Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it."﴾ Some read "yubdilana" with light pronunciation, and both are two dialects. Some distinguished between them, saying: al-tabdil is changing the state and attribute of a thing while the substance remains, and al-ibdal is removing a thing and putting something else in its place. It is related that the people sincerely repented, so God gave them a garden in which a single cluster was a load for a mule.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Such is the punishment﴾, meaning what We did to them, We will do to whoever transgresses Our limits. Here ends the story of the people of the garden. Then the Exalted said: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾, meaning the polytheists. Then He mentioned what awaits the God-fearing in His presence in what follows. The polytheists said: "Indeed, we will be given in the Hereafter better than what you are given." So the Exalted said, denying them: ﴿Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: this alif of interrogation here has the function of rebuke and affirmation.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿How do you judge?﴾, that is, how do you decide with injustice? ﴿Or do you have a Book﴾ sent down from God ﴿in which you study﴾, that is, you read what is in it, ﴿that indeed for you in it is whatever you choose﴾, that is, whatever you select and desire. Abu al-Jawza', 'Asim al-Jahdari, and Abu 'Imran read "anna lakum" with a fatha on the hamza. This is a reproach to them and a rebuke for what they wish for of falsehood. ["Ask them which of them will guarantee that"]. ﴿Or do you have oaths binding upon Us until the Day of Resurrection﴾, that is, do you have covenants with God, the Exalted, in which He swore to you regarding what you claim, with binding oaths, that is, emphatic oaths. Everything that is complete in excellence and soundness is "baligh" (binding). It is also possible that the meaning is: binding until the Day of Resurrection, that is, those oaths reach to the Day of Resurrection in their obligation and their confirmation. ["Indeed, for you is what you judge"], meaning that for yourselves you have from it good and honour with [p-340] God the Exalted. Al-Farra' said: the readers read "balighatun" with a raised ending except al-Hasan, who put it in the accusative, following the manner of the verbal noun, as in His statement: ﴿truly (haqqan)﴾ [al-Rum 47]. The meaning of the verse is: "Do you have oaths binding upon Us that for you is what you judge?!" Since the lam was in the answer to "inna", he kasra'd it.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Ask them which of them will guarantee that﴾. On this there are two views.

The first: that it is the guarantor (al-kafil). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. The meaning is: which of them undertook that for them in the Hereafter there is the good that belongs to the Muslims.

it intends the intention of the garden that is closed off."

That is, it intends its intention. Ibn Qutaybah said: there are two dialects in it, harad and hard, as one says al-darak and al-darak.

The second: capable over the poor. This was said by al-Sha'bi.

One says to another, "You advised us," and the other says, "You did it." Then they called out against themselves with woe, and they said: ﴿"Woe to us! Some distinguished between them, saying: al-tabdil is changing the state and attribute of a thing while the substance remains, and al-ibdal is removing a thing and putting something else in its place. it intends the intention of the garden that is closed off."

One says to another, "You advised us," and the other says, "You did it." Then they called out against themselves with woe, and they said: ﴿"Woe to us! Some distinguished between them, saying: al-tabdil is changing the state and attribute of a thing while the substance remains, and al-ibdal is removing a thing and putting something else in its place. The partners were attributed to them only because of their claim that they are partners of God.

[p-336] The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have tested them﴾ means the people of Makkah, that is, We tested them with hunger and famine, ﴿as We tested the owners of the garden﴾ when their garden was destroyed.

This is a reference to their story. The people of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) mentioned that there was a man in the region of Yemen who had a garden, and he was a believer. This was after 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon them both. He would take from it only enough for his sustenance and would give away the rest in charity. It was also said that he would leave for the poor what the sickle passed over, what fell from the tops of the palm trees, and what scattered during threshing. A considerable amount would accumulate from this. Then the man died and left three sons. They said: "By God, the wealth is little and the dependents are many. Our father only did this when the wealth was abundant and the dependents few, but now we cannot do this." So they resolved to deprive the poor, and they made a pact among themselves that they would go out early, before people went out, and cut their palm trees. This is the meaning of His statement: ﴿when they swore﴾, that is, they took an oath, ﴿that they would surely harvest it﴾, that is, they would surely cut their palm trees, ﴿in the early morning﴾, that is, at the first light of dawn. Some darkness of the night still remained, so that nothing would be left for the poor.

Regarding His statement ﴿and they did not make an exception﴾ there are two views.

The first: they did not say, "If God wills." This is the view of most scholars.

The second: they did not make an exception for the right of the poor. This was said by 'Ikrimah.

[p-337] ﴿Then there passed over it a visitation from your Lord﴾, that is, from the command of your Lord. Al-Farra' said: the visitation can only occur at night. The exegetes said: God sent a fire upon it at night, and it was burned and became black. This is the meaning of His statement: ﴿so it became like the darkened [garden]﴾. On this there are three views.

The first: it became like black ash. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it became like the blackened night. This was said by al-Farra'. Likewise Ibn Qutaybah said: it became black like the night, burned. Al-Layl (the night) is also called al-sarim, and al-subh (the morning) is also called sarim, because each of them is cut off (yanṣarim) from the other.

The third: it became morning and the fruit in it had gone, so it was as if it had been cut off (ṣurima), that is, cut and harvested. This was also related by Ibn Qutaybah.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Then they called to one another at dawn﴾, that is, some of them called to others when they had risen in the morning, ["Go early to your tilth"], meaning the fruits, crops and grapes, ﴿if you are going to harvest﴾, that is, if you are going to cut the palm trees. ﴿So they set out﴾, that is, they went to their garden, ﴿while they whispered﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: they spoke secretly, [saying], ["No poor person shall enter it upon you today"], ﴿and they went early with determination﴾. On this there are eight views.

[p-338] The first: with capability. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: with want. This was said by al-Hasan in one narration.

The third: with seriousness. This was said by al-Hasan in another narration, and by Qatadah, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Farra', and Muqatil.

The fourth: with a matter that was agreed upon and that they had established among themselves. This was said by Mujahid and 'Ikrimah.

The fifth: that al-harad is the name of the garden. This was said by al-Suddi.

The sixth: that it is anger and wrath against the poor. This was said by al-Sha'bi and Sufyan. Abu 'Ubaydah recited:

"Lions of a den met the hidden lions,
they gave one another to drink, in anger, the blood of lions."

The seventh: that it is prevention, derived from "the year was harad" when there was no rain in it, and "the she-camel was harad" when she had no milk. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah.

The eighth: that it is intention. One says, "I haradtu your harad," meaning, I intended your intention. This was related by al-Farra', Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah. They recited:

"A torrent has come from the command of God,
it intends the intention of the garden that is closed off."

That is, it intends its intention. Ibn Qutaybah said: there are two dialects in it, harad and hard, as one says al-darak and al-darak.

Regarding His statement ﴿capable﴾ there are three views.

The first: capable of their garden in their own estimation. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: capable over the poor. This was said by al-Sha'bi.

The third: the meaning is that they prevented while they were able, that is, they had the means. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

They said, ﴿when they saw it﴾ burned, ﴿"Indeed, we have gone astray."﴾ That is, we have lost the way to our garden, for this is not it. Then they realized it was a punishment, so they said: ﴿"Rather, we are deprived."﴾ That is, we were deprived of the fruit of our garden by withholding from the poor. ﴿The most just of them said﴾, that is, the most upright and the best of them. ﴿"Why did you not"﴾, that is, "Would that you had," ﴿"glorify [God]"﴾. On this there are three views.

The first: "Why did you not make an exception when you said: ['We will surely harvest it in the early morning']." This was said by Ibn Jurayj and the majority. The meaning is: "Why did you not say, 'If God wills'?" The exception is a magnification of God and an acknowledgement that no one can do an act except by the will of God.

The second: their exception was the statement "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to God). This was said by Abu Salih.

The third: "Why do you not glorify God and thank Him for what He has given you?" This was related by al-Tha'labi.

[p-339] The statement of the Exalted: ﴿They said, "Glory be to our Lord"﴾, so they declared Him free from being unjust in what He did, and they confessed against themselves to wrongdoing, so they said: ﴿"Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾ By withholding from the poor. One says to another, "You advised us," and the other says, "You did it." Then they called out against themselves with woe, and they said: ﴿"Woe to us! Indeed, we were transgressors."﴾ Because we did not do what our fathers did. Then they returned to God the Exalted and asked Him to replace it for them with something better. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 68, verses 42–47:

﴿On the day when [the matter] is laid bare﴾. The meaning is: let them bring it [the proof] on the day when ﴿the shin is laid bare﴾. The majority of reciters read *yukshafu* (يُكْشَفُ) with a *ḍamma* on the *yā'* and a *fatḥa* on the *shīn*, meaning the passive form. Ibn Abi 'Abla, 'Asim al-Jahdari, and Abu al-Jawza' read it with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'* and a *kasra* on the *shīn*, meaning the active form. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas read *takshifu* (تَكْشِفُ) with an open *tā'* and a *kasra* on the *shīn*. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn Ya'mar, and al-Dahhak read *nakshifu* (نَكْشِفُ) with an open *nūn* and a *kasra* on the *shīn*. (p-٣٤١) This day is the Day of Resurrection. 'Ikrima related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿the day when the shin is laid bare﴾ that he said: it means that [the matter] is laid bare of severity. He recited:

"War has stood up against us on the shin."

This is also the view of Mujahid and Qatada.

Ibn Qutayba said: The origin of this is that when a man falls into a great matter that requires him to exert himself and strive earnestly in it, he rolls up his shin (leg). The shin is thus borrowed for the place of severity. This is the view of al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayda, and the lexicographers. This matter has been attributed to Allah the Exalted. It is related in the *Sahihayn* (the two *Sahih* collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet (ﷺ) said that [Allah] "lays bare His shin." This is an attribution to Him, because the whole [matter] belongs to Him and the action is His. Abu 'Umar al-Zahid said: It is meant to refer to the self (nafs). From this is the saying of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "I fight them even if my shin is destroyed," meaning my self. On this view, the meaning is that He will manifest Himself to them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they will be called to prostration﴾. It means the hypocrites. ﴿But they will not be able﴾. As if there were rods of iron in their backs. Al-Naqqash said: This is not a command to them to prostrate, since they are incapable, but it is a rebuke for them for abandoning prostration. ﴿Their eyes will be humbled﴾, that is, submissive. ﴿Humiliation will cover them﴾, that is, will overwhelm them. ﴿And they used to be called to prostration﴾, meaning by the call (adhan) in the abode of this world, and they were commanded to perform the obligatory prayer (al-salat al-maktuba). ﴿While they were sound﴾, that is, healthy, having in their loins nothing like rods of iron. In this there is a warning for those who abandon the congregational prayer. Ka'b used to say: By Allah, this verse was only revealed concerning those who lag behind from the congregations.

﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse﴾, meaning the Qur'an. The meaning is: leave Me to deal with him. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, do not occupy your heart with him; entrust him to Me, for I will suffice you in his affair. Some exegetes mentioned that this portion of the verse, up to His saying "the discourse," was abrogated by the verse of the sword. What follows this is explained in [al-A'raf: 182–183], up to His saying the Exalted: ﴿Or do you ask them for a reward﴾, for it is explained there, and the verse before it is explained in [al-Tur: 39–40].

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 68, verses 48–52:**

God's words: ﴿So be patient for the judgement of your Lord﴾. That is: be patient over their harm until the decree of your Lord, which is coming, is carried out. It has been said: the command to be patient is abrogated (*naskh*, the cancellation of one ruling by a later one) by the verse of the sword.

God's words: ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾, who is Yunus (Jonah). Scholars differ on what he was forbidden to be like in this, and there are two views.

The first: it is haste and anger, as Qatadah said.

The second: it is weakness in conveying the message, as Ibn Jarir said.

Ibn al-Anbari said: This does not remove Yunus from the *Ulu al-Azm* (the possessors of steadfast resolve, the most exalted prophets), because it was a lapse. (p-343) If we said that every prophet who erred is not among the *Ulu al-Azm*, then all of them would be excluded except Yahya. Then he (God) informed about his punishment for not being patient, so He said: ﴿When he called out while he was distressed﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: *makzum* means filled with grief and anguish.

God's words: ﴿Had not a blessing from his Lord reached him﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "*Law la an tadarakathu*" with a light *ta'* and a sukun *ta'* after the *kaf*, with the *dal* lightened. Abu Hurayra and Abu al-Mutawakkil read: "*Taddarakahu*" with one light *ta'* and a stressed *dal*. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "*Tatadarakahu*" with two light *ta'*s. ﴿A blessing from his Lord﴾: so He showed him mercy and accepted his repentance for his disobediences. ﴿He would have been cast onto the open wasteland while blameworthy﴾. The meaning of *al-'ara'* (the open wasteland) has been explained in [al-Saffat: 145]. The meaning of the verse is: he was cast out not blameworthy, because of God's blessing upon him through repentance and mercy. Ibn Jurayj said: ("cast onto the open wasteland") refers to the land of the Gathering, meaning he would have remained in that place until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then his Lord chose him﴾: that is, He selected him, chose him, and cleared him of blame, ﴿so He made him among the righteous﴾. So He returned revelation to him and granted intercession for his people and himself.

God's words: ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve almost make you slip with their eyes﴾. Most readers recited it with a *damma* on the *ya'* from *azlaqtuhu* (to make someone slip). The people of Madina and Aban recited it with a *fatha* from *zalaqtuhu azlquhu* (to slip). Both are well-known dialects among the Arabs. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said *zalaqa al-rajul ra'sahu wa azlaqahu* when he shaved his head.

On the meaning of the verse, the commentators have two views.

The first: "The disbelievers intended to afflict the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with the evil eye. Among them was a man who would remain for two or three days without eating anything, then he would raise the side of his tent, and the camels would pass by him. He would say: I have not seen today camels or sheep more beautiful than these. Not long after, a number of them would fall dead. The disbelievers asked this man to afflict the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with the evil eye, so God protected His Prophet and revealed this verse." This is the view of al-Kalbi, and a group of commentators followed him, having taken this from his exegesis, among them al-Farra'.

The second: they used to look at him with intense hostility, a look so severe that it nearly made him slip, that is, cast him to the ground because of its intensity. This is used in the speech of the Arabs. A speaker says: So-and-so looked at me with a look that almost knocked me down. They recited:

"They exchange looks when they meet in a place,
a look that removes the places of the feet."

That is, some of them look at others with an intense look of hostility that almost removes their feet. This is the view taken by the careful scholars (*al-muhaqqiqun*), among them Ibn Qutayba and al-Zajjaj. What supports its soundness is that God linked this look with hearing the Qur'an, as in His words: ﴿When they heard the Reminder﴾. The people disliked that most intensely, so they fixed their gaze upon him with hatred. The affliction of the evil eye occurs only with admiration and approval, not with hatred, so it cannot be assumed that al-Kalbi understood the meaning of the verse.

﴿And it is not﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿except a reminder﴾, that is, an admonition.
